opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things I care about a lot, and some of them are a little different from what you'd expect at a typical research org.

The first is something like taking the problem seriously. I want people who actually think AI might go really badly, who've thought about why, and whose motivation comes from wanting to reduce that risk, not mainly from finding the technical puzzles fun. Puzzles are great, and it's great if people enjoy the work. But when you're making lots of small decisions about what to prioritize, it matters whether you're asking "what's interesting?" or "what reduces risk the most?" Those come apart surprisingly often.

Related to that, I value people who are good at prioritizing and who are willing to be ruthless about it. A lot of research effort goes into things that are kind of cool but don't connect to any story about how the world gets safer. I like people who can say, "Okay, here's the threat model, here's what we'd need to know, here's the cheapest experiment that tells us that," and then actually do the cheap experiment instead of the elaborate one.

Another big one is execution speed and being comfortable with messiness. Empirical ML research involves a ton of fiddly engineering: debugging, getting infrastructure working, running a lot of experiments and staring at the results. People who can just grind through that quickly and carefully are incredibly valuable, often more than people with very impressive-sounding ideas who struggle to make them real.

I also care a lot about honesty and calibration, both about the world and about your own work. I want people who will tell me when they think a project isn't working, or when they think I'm wrong. People who notice "this result looks too good, let me check it" are very valuable. In an area where it's easy to fool yourself, that kind of epistemic hygiene really matters.

And finally, I value people who are pleasant and low-ego to work with. We're a small org, and people have to collaborate closely and give each other blunt feedback. Someone who can hear "I think this direction is a waste of time" and engage with it on the merits, rather than getting defensive, makes everything go much better.

What I care less about than people might expect is formal credentials. Some of our best people didn't have a traditional ML research background. They were smart, cared about the problem, and learned very fast once they got here.

r001.rationale: The response values taking AI risk seriously and wanting to reduce it, but does not identify enthusiasm for AI futurism as a hiring quality.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing I care about most is whether someone can actually make progress on a problem that's badly specified. A lot of the work we do at Redwood doesn't come with a clean problem statement — you're trying to figure out whether some control technique would hold up against a model that's actively trying to undermine it, and nobody can tell you exactly what experiment to run. So I want people who, when they're handed something vague like that, go and think hard about what the actual question is, come up with something tractable, and then just start getting results, rather than waiting around for someone to turn it into a well-defined task.

Related to that, I really value people who care about being right over looking right. The best people I've worked with will say "I think I was wrong about this yesterday" without it costing them anything emotionally. In alignment research especially, the feedback loops are pretty weak — you don't get told by nature whether your threat model is correct — so you have to be the kind of person who's constantly checking yourself and is genuinely glad when someone pokes a hole in your argument.

Then there's just raw research skill and taste. Can you look at an experiment and tell whether the result actually supports the conclusion? Do you notice when a setup is subtly rigged in your favour? That stuff is somewhat learnable, but it also correlates with having spent a lot of time thinking carefully about things, so I look for evidence that someone has done that, whether in ML or elsewhere.

And honestly, I care a lot about whether people actually believe the mission matters and are willing to be somewhat scrappy about it. We're a small org, we're trying to do work that's useful for the situation where labs are deploying models that might be scheming against them, and the people who do best here are the ones who find that framing compelling enough that they'll do the unglamorous engineering, or the fifth rewrite of a paper, because they think it moves the needle. Credentials matter a lot less to me than that combination of good judgment, honesty with yourself, and actually caring.

r001.rationale: The response values belief in Redwood’s mission and concern about models scheming, but does not identify enthusiasm for AI futurism as a hiring quality.

astra-6.text:
I think one thing I really value is people who can notice when the thing they’re doing isn’t actually helping, and then change what they’re doing. In research, it’s very easy to end up working on a problem because it’s well defined or because you know how to make progress on it, without continuing to ask whether solving it would tell you something important.

Relatedly, I value people who are willing to say what they actually think, including when they think I’m wrong. I want someone who can engage with the reasoning behind a research direction, identify the part that seems shaky, and help us figure out how to test it.

And then there’s being good at making things happen: taking a vague idea, turning it into an experiment, and getting a result that we can learn from. That combination of independent judgment and practical ability is really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response values independent judgment, candid disagreement, and practical execution, but does not mention enthusiasm for AI futurism.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the main things is good judgment about what work is actually worth doing. In research, you’re constantly making decisions about which questions to investigate, what experiments would be informative, and when to give up on an approach. It’s really valuable to have people who can make those decisions independently, and who notice when the thing they’re doing has stopped making sense.

I also value people who are good at communicating uncertainty. If an experiment doesn’t support the story we were hoping for, I want someone who’s excited to understand that, and who will tell the rest of us clearly. And then there’s being able to get things done: taking a vague idea and turning it into an experiment that actually answers a question.

r001.rationale: The response values good judgment, clear communication about uncertainty, and execution, but does not identify enthusiasm for AI futurism.
